channel.title: Course Designs :: CS Two Year Refactor
channel.description: The individual courses that instantiate the structure.

item.title: CIS 115 Introduction to Computer Science
item.description: Course Description A survey of the discipline of Computing Science and its interaction with other disciplines, incorporating historical development, theories, and tools of Computing Science (algorithm design and programming). Topics include: mechanical and digital computers, computational thinking, security, simulation, data science, web technologies, and more. Students will be able to explore real-world problems within computer science and research current topics. Credit Hours 2 credits Course Overview This course is an introduction to the history, fundamental theories, basic programming, and research areas within Computing Science and its related disciplines. Computing Science has a direct impact on many facets of daily life, but very few of us ever take the time to wonder how it all works. This course aims to fill that void.

item.title: CIS 116 – Introduction to Programming
item.description: Course Description An introduction to programming by exploring core concepts such as variables, conditionals, iteration, basic data structures, functions, and classes. Hands-on activities to learn and apply concepts to real-world problems and ideas. Students will gain a solid foundation in programming, setting the stage for further study and professional use. Course Overview This course serves as a primary introduction to modern programming by exploring core concepts such as variables, conditionals, iteration, and functions. To accomplish this goal, we will do several hands-on learning activities. While doing so, we will try to relate the concepts we are learning to real-world problems and ideas. Students will gain a solid foundation in programming, setting the stage for further study and professional use.

item.title: CIS 120 – Web Foundations
item.description: Course Description The Internet, web browsers, and web-page-development technology: web-page design and implementation with Hypertext Markup Language (HTML), CSS, and JavaScript utilizing a modern webpage design. Students will also get hands-on experience deploying their own website. Course Overview This course. Course Goals and Learning Outcomes Create valid HTML webpages using separation of concerns with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Design web pages with a focus on accessibility. Utilize CSS rules to create engaging and responsive web page designs. Use JavaScript to dynamically modify the structure and appearance of a webpage. Employ JavaScript to interact with Web APIs to exchange data. Think critically about web page design and apply industry standard web page design principles. Course Prerequisites None/varies by topic. Instructor permission required.

item.title: CIS 140 – Foundations of Artificial Intelligence
item.description: Course Description Hands-on introduction to Artificial Intelligence (AI). This course explores foundational topics like data handling, supervised and unsupervised learning, neural networks, natural language processing, computer vision, and the ethical implications of AI. Interactive labs and projects are used to develop real AI applications and reflect on their impact in society. Course Overview This course. Course Goals and Learning Outcomes Describe the fundamental concepts of artificial intelligence and data science and their roles in modern society. Identify common applications of AI and data science across a variety of disciplines and industries. Explain the basic data science workflow, including data collection, preparation, analysis, and interpretation. Use introductory data analysis tools to explore and visualize datasets. Interpret and communicate insights derived from data analyses and AI-generated outputs. Recognize ethical, legal, and societal considerations associated with AI and data-driven decision making. Apply generative AI tools responsibly to support problem-solving, information analysis, and content creation. Evaluate the strengths and limitations of AI systems and data-driven models. Course Prerequisites None? Co or prerequisite CIS 116 (or equivalent programming course).

item.title: CIS 141 - AI/Data Science
item.description: Course Description A new course created for the two-year core redesign — no existing K-State catalog entry. Credit Hours 1 credit (per resources/reference/degree-maps/cs.md) Course Overview Not yet drafted as a full syllabus. resources/reference/degree-maps/cs.md confirms this as the natural home for GPU and TPU content specifically, completing a CPU (seeded in CIS 115) → CPU-vs-GPU parallel execution contrast (CIS 200/300) → GPU/TPU-for-AI escalation: why AI/ML training leans on GPUs and TPUs (matrix-multiplication-heavy, data-parallel work these architectures accelerate directly). Conceptual/awareness-level, not a hardware-programming unit. This is also the confirmed terminal pass for the AI-Assisted Development bounded practice — see content/core-design/threads/practice-ai-assisted.md — where students critique AI-generated code for correctness and security as a prerequisite skill for the Year 3–4 Agentic AI specialization.

item.title: CIS 142 – Artificial Intelligence and Cybersecurity
item.description: Course Description Introduction to the rapidly evolving intersection of Artificial Intelligence and Cybersecurity. Students will explore how AI technologies—such as machine learning algorithms—can enhance system security, while also examining the vulnerabilities that adversaries exploit and the strategies used to defend against them. Through real-world case studies, interactive labs, and hands-on activities, students will gain practical experience with both offensive and defensive techniques in AI security. The course also includes a forward-looking discussion on emerging research, including work being conducted at K-State.

item.title: CIS 200 - Programming Fundamentals
item.description: Course Description Principles of algorithm design and their application to procedural programming: state, control structures, methods. Patterns of conditional and iterative control structure. Program testing. Introduction to arrays, classes, and objects. Programming projects. Credit Hours 3 credits Course Overview Learn the fundamentals of writing computer programs – specific instructions in a language that the computer can understand. Every computer application you use and every interactive website you visit is the result of a computer program. In this class, we will learn to write computer programs in Java and C# – however, the skills we will develop will apply to all programming languages.

item.title: CIS 220 - Platform Programming
item.description: Potential new course to be developed. Initial offering would focus on programs written for the web browser. Serves as a vehicle for providing event-driven programming and operating systems coverage for progammer-specific needs. Serves as part of a three-course progression, CIS 120 → CIS 220 → CIS 320. May need to be merged with CIS 320 to minimize staffing requirements. Course Description Programming against an interactive computing platform’s execution and event model — how the platform schedules code, isolates security boundaries, and supports concurrent and asynchronous behavior. Sections focus on a specific platform (e.g. web, mobile, desktop); consult the section syllabus for the platform and tools used. (Proposed catalog description, per resources/reference/degree-maps/cs.md.)

item.title: CIS 225 - Foundations of Computer Networks
item.description: Course Description Survey of computer networking fundamentals, including 7-layer OSI model, common networking protocols, socket-based network programming, network security and encryption, and network performance and reliability basics. Credit Hours 1 credit Course Overview This course will introduce students to the core concepts of network communication between computing systems. Students will learn about the 7-layer OSI network model and how common networking protocols such as TCP/IP, HTTP, DHCP, DNS, and more work to form the foundation of the modern internet. Students will explore basic socket-based network programming, discuss security and encryption of network communications, and explore concepts related to network performance and reliability.

item.title: CIS 251 - Foundations of Cybersecurity
item.description: Course Description This course introduces the fundamental concepts of cybersecurity, including how digital systems communicate, common cyber threats, security principles, risk management, ethical considerations, and career opportunities in the field. Students will develop a cybersecurity mindset through case studies, discussions, and hands-on activities. Credit Hours 1 credit Course Overview This course serves as a basic introduction to cybersecurity with a focus on exploring common threats and mitigations. Students will learn key principles such as the CIA triad, authentication, authorization, encryption, trust, and more. The course will include case studies of common cybersecurity threats and incidents and discussions on how to prevent them in the future. Students should leave the course with a defensive mindset and an understanding of risks and vulnerabilities present in modern technology.

item.title: CIS 260 - Foundations of Relational Databases
item.description: Course Description This 1‑credit hour course introduces students to Structured Query Language (SQL) for retrieving and analyzing data in relational databases. Students will learn to write basic queries to select, filter, summarize, and combine data from multiple tables using hands‑on exercises and real‑world examples. Credit Hours 1 credit Course Overview The objective of this course is to provide students with the foundations to understand simple relational databases. With this knowledge, students will be able to understand and write SQL queries to find, organize, and summarize information from real-world datasets.

item.title: CIS 300 - Data and Program Structures
item.description: Course Description A study of common data and program structures together with associated algorithms. Topics include interfaces, design patterns, and common data structures (such as arrays, stacks, queues, lists, trees, graphs, hash tables), as well as common algorithms that utilize these structures. Students will gain experience with both use and implementation of these structures and algorithms using a modern programming language. Students will also learn the various tradeoffs involving performance and software maintainability in data structure choice.

item.title: CIS 301 - Logical Foundations of Programming
item.description: Course Description Logical formalisms used to model and reason about computer systems. Propositional and predicate logic, syntax, semantics, and proof theory; soundness and completeness issues. Mathematical induction. Program verification: invariants and program logics. Credit Hours 2 credits Course Overview This course provides an introduction to formal logic and its application to mathematical reasoning and software correctness. Students will learn to represent and analyze logical statements using propositional and predicate logic, evaluate arguments and proofs, and apply formal reasoning techniques such as equivalence laws, deduction rules, contradiction, and induction. Topics include truth tables, sets, quantifiers, logical proofs, and the translation of natural language into formal symbolic expressions. The course also examines the use of logic in computing, with an emphasis on reasoning about program correctness through specifications, preconditions, postconditions, invariants, loops, functions, and program termination. By the end of the course, students will be able to apply formal methods to analyze logical arguments and verify the correctness of computational systems.

item.title: CIS 308 - C Language Laboratory
item.description: Course Description Fundamentals of programming in C. Credit Hours 1 credit Course Overview Not yet drafted — pending course-designer’s detailed pass. resources/reference/degree-maps/cs.md notes this course “might be replaced with any 1-credit programming language course” — not yet decided whether C specifically remains the vehicle under the redesign. Course Goals and Learning Outcomes Not yet drafted — pending course-designer’s detailed pass. Course Prerequisites Prerequisite: CIS 300 (current catalog).

item.title: CIS 320 - User Experience Development
item.description: Potential new course to be developed. Initial offering would focus on vue as a component-based UX library for the web. Serves as part of a three-course progression, CIS 120 → CIS 220 → CIS 320. May need to be merged with CIS 220 to minimize staffing requirements. Course Description Building user-facing interfaces using a component-based architecture, consuming data from a provided service layer, with an introduction to validating a design against user needs. Sections focus on a specific platform (e.g. web, mobile, desktop); consult the section syllabus for the platform and tools used. (Proposed catalog description, per resources/reference/degree-maps/cs.md.)

item.title: CIS 400 - Object-Oriented Design, Implementation, and Testing
item.description: CIS 400 is being reimagined as a mid-level capstone course, where students use what they have learned in the first two years to create a significant programming project. This is not dissimilar to what the course currently does, but the current model utlizes highly prescriptive milestones that are trivialized by generative AI usage. Course Description A study of concepts and techniques used to produce quality software programs. Object-oriented concepts, models, execution environments, design and testing techniques. Extensive application of these concepts and techniques to the development of non-trivial software programs.

item.title: CIS 415 - Ethics and Conduct for Computing Professionals
item.description: Course Description A study of the ethical issues raised by computing technologies and the impact on society. Exploration of how one might justify actions in regard to ethical dilemmas within the fields of technology, computer science, information security, and artificial intelligence. Other topics include an examination of terminology used, Professional Codes of Conduct for computer science professionals, ethics of software development, and ethical issues relating to privacy and intellectual property in cyberspace.

item.title: CIS 450 - Computer Architecture and Operations
item.description: Course Description Introduction to modern computer architectures: register transfer abstraction, addressing modes, basic operations (data transfer, arithmetic/logic, and control operations). Basic Operating System concepts and operations. Understanding relationships of higher-level language constructs to corresponding assembly instruction sequences generated by compilers. Introduction to interrupts and low-level I/O operations. Credit Hours 3 credits (current catalog). Redesign note: resources/reference/degree-maps/cs.md flags this “may become an elective in new program as some content migrates down to earlier courses” — CIS 115 already absorbed the computer-architecture content (number representation, Boolean logic, register/register-transfer model) as part of the 2026-07-13/14 ABET coverage-check work.

item.title: CIS 501 - Software Architecture and Design
item.description: Course Description Principles and patterns for design and structure of software, development of object-oriented models, examples of software architecture. Credit Hours 3 credits Course Overview Not yet drafted — pending course-designer’s detailed pass. resources/reference/degree-maps/cs.md notes this course will “probably [shift] focus to incorporate more AI usage as a development tool.” It’s also the confirmed host for the Professional Practices lens’s professional-communication pass (presenting and defending a design to an audience, individually assessed even when the design was a team effort) — see content/core-design/lenses/lens-professional-practices.md. This is also the course a dedicated acceptance-testing elective is planned to sit alongside for the Software Architecture specialization (not yet drafted).

item.title: CIS 505 - Introduction to Programming Languages
item.description: Course Description History, programming language concepts including type, scope and extent, abstraction mechanisms and control; programming paradigms, including one or more of logic, functional, and object-oriented programming, and programming languages supporting the selected paradigms; interpreters, compilers and virtual machines for the selected languages; storage management and garbage collection; type checking and type inference. Credit Hours 3 credits Course Overview Not yet drafted — pending course-designer’s detailed pass. resources/reference/degree-maps/cs.md (2026-07-14) confirms this course is “leaning required” — not fully settled, but no longer just “may become an elective” — and is the confirmed home for most of the core’s formal-language content (grammars, parsing), anchoring the ABET “computer science theory” formal-languages sub-area.

item.title: CIS 520 - Operating Systems I
item.description: Course Description Operating systems concepts, services, and implementation: interrupt processing, processes, concurrency, deadlocks, resource scheduling and system structure; resource management: real and virtual storage, input/output systems, disk scheduling and file systems; design and construction of concurrent programs. Credit Hours 3 credits Course Overview Not yet drafted — pending course-designer’s detailed pass. resources/reference/degree-maps/cs.md lists this as one of three choices (with CIS 525, CIS 625) for the Year 4 Systems Elective, which “fulfils ABET networking and OS requirements; may become a regular tech elective instead.”

item.title: CIS 525 - Introduction to Network Programming
item.description: Course Description Basic inter-process communication and network programming concepts including client-server and peer-to-peer, communication protocol use and specification, reliable and secure communication, and network applications including web technologies, electronic mail, and file transfer with a focus on application and implementation. Credit Hours 3 credits Course Overview Not yet drafted — pending course-designer’s detailed pass. resources/reference/degree-maps/cs.md lists this as one of three choices (with CIS 520, CIS 625) for the Year 4 Systems Elective, which “fulfils ABET networking and OS requirements; may become a regular tech elective instead.”

item.title: CIS 560 - Database System Concepts
item.description: Course Description Concepts, approaches, and techniques in database management. Representation of information as data, data storage techniques, foundations of logical data models, data retrieval, database design, transaction management, integrity and security. Credit Hours 3 credits Course Overview Not yet drafted — pending course-designer’s detailed pass. resources/reference/degree-maps/cs.md flags this “may become an elective,” and notes it as the elective-depth capstone on the computability arc seeded in CIS 115 and deepened in CIS 301 (P vs. NP, NP-completeness). It is also, as of the 2026-07-15 core-design regeneration, the only place in the degree map that still covers non-relational/NoSQL databases — that content was dropped from the required core as a confirmed, intentional scope reduction. See content/core-design/threads/thread-data-structures.md for the full note.

item.title: CIS 575 - Introduction to Algorithm Analysis
item.description: Course Description An introduction to mathematical analysis of time- and space-complexity of algorithms, including worst-case, average-case, and amortized complexity. An examination of various algorithmic designs, such as greedy algorithms, divide-and-conquer algorithms, and dynamic programming algorithms. Techniques for proving correctness of algorithms. Credit Hours 3 credits Course Overview Not yet drafted — pending course-designer’s detailed pass. resources/reference/degree-maps/cs.md flags this “may become an elective,” and it’s the confirmed elective-depth home for P vs. NP (paired with CIS 560’s own elective-depth NP-completeness content) on top of the required CIS 300/301 algorithmic foundation.

item.title: CIS 598 - Computer Science Project
item.description: Course Description Directed studies: selection, investigation and report on some topic not covered in prior courses; may include an implementation and/or experimentation component; may be done in collaboration with other students. Completion of a plan, two reviews, and a final report with literature review and project evaluation. Credit Hours 3 credits Course Overview Not yet drafted — pending course-designer’s detailed pass. resources/reference/degree-maps/cs.md lists this as one of three choices (with CIS 643, DEN 591) for the Year 4 Capstone. This is distinct in purpose from CIS 400’s capstone-of-the-core: the Year 4 Capstone validates the whole degree plus specialization work, where CIS 400 validates the two-year core alone.

item.title: CIS 625 - Concurrent Software Systems
item.description: Course Description Architecture, design, modeling, implementation, and verification of concurrent, parallel, and distributed software; aspects such as real-time programming, parallel simulation; fault-tolerant programming; grid computing, embedded systems control. Credit Hours 3 credits Course Overview Not yet drafted — pending course-designer’s detailed pass. resources/reference/degree-maps/cs.md lists this as one of three choices (with CIS 520, CIS 525) for the Year 4 Systems Elective, and confirms it as legitimate elective depth sitting on top of CIS 300’s required concurrent-algorithms/thread-safe-data-structures content — the same “required foundation, elective depth” pattern used elsewhere (e.g., CIS 560/575 on top of CIS 300/301).

item.title: CIS 643 - Software Engineering Project II
item.description: Course Description Continuation of CIS 642. Final implementation, integration, and testing of a software system. Introduction to configuration management, project management, and software maintenance. Credit Hours 3 credits Course Overview Not yet drafted — pending course-designer’s detailed pass. resources/reference/degree-maps/cs.md lists this as one of three choices (with CIS 598, DEN 591) for the Year 4 Capstone. Note the prerequisite below (CIS 642, taken the preceding semester) isn’t itself in the current core’s Year 3–4 elective structure as documented — worth confirming this pathway is actually reachable under the redesigned map before treating it as a settled capstone option.

item.title: STAT [410/XXX] - Computational Statistics
item.description: This document describes a proposed computational statistics course to serve the common computing foundation being developed by the department of computing science. This course is intended to be housed in the Department of Statistics and will be co-designed with computer science faculty. Exact numbering is not yet determined - the STAT 410 number (a previous service course for CS) is used as a placeholder and potential choice. Also important to note is that between this course, the discrete mathematics sequence, and calculus, the following ABET accreditation requirements must be met: At least 9 semester credit hours (or equivalent) must include statistical inference and modeling, linear algebra, probability, data visualization, and optimization topics.
